extracted.intended_audience: communications researchers and practitioners, policy advocates, and social-change professionals interested in evidence-based framing and strategic communications
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply the Strategic Frame Analysis (SFA) research approach: a multimethod, multidisciplinary, iterative research trajectory that produces empirical evidence about framing effects to inform evidence-based communications for complex social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five major phases of Strategic Frame Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The article describes the five major phases of research associated with Strategic Frame Analysis, an approach to communications research and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper presents a research trajectory composed of five major phases; these phases together form the SFA research cycle and are discussed as an ordered sequence that researchers follow when investigating framing for social change. (The page references the existence and logical ordering of these phases but does not enumerate them in this summary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimethod research approach
rubrics_metrics.description: SFA is characterized as a multimethod approach to communications research and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple complementary research methods rather than a single method when studying frames and framing effects — combining qualitative and quantitative techniques to build and test framing hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multidisciplinary techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach emphasizes multidisciplinary research techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on insights and methods from multiple disciplines (e.g., cognitive science, linguistics, sociology, political communication) to analyze and design frames; incorporate disciplinary diversity into study design and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative research process
rubrics_metrics.description: Research techniques within SFA are iterative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt iterative cycles of testing, refinement, and retesting of frames and messages rather than one-off studies; allow findings to feed back into new hypothesis generation and message design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing of potential frame effects
rubrics_metrics.description: SFA gives emphasis to empirical testing of potential frame effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize experiments, observational studies, or other empirical designs that can detect whether proposed frames produce the intended cognitive or behavioral effects; use empirical evidence to choose and refine communications strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic and ordering of methods in the research cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: The logic behind the constellation of methods and the order in which they are taken up in the research cycle is important to SFA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a planned sequence of methods (e.g., formative qualitative work → message development → experimental testing → field trials) so that each method builds on prior findings; justify methodological sequencing as part of evidence-based communications design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on entrenched and complex social problems
rubrics_metrics.description: SFA is intended to advance new ways of pursuing social change of entrenched and complex social problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design framing research with the goal of addressing deep-seated, complex policy or social issues; consider system-level constraints and long-term change pathways when interpreting framing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing the 'evidence' for evidence-based communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach aims to provide the empirical 'evidence' required for evidence-based communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame research and reporting to generate clear, actionable evidence that practitioners and policymakers can use to inform communications strategies; document methods and results to support evidence claims.
